When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 14 percent chose one of the five legislative ballot measures (7% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 2% Proposition 4; 2% Proposition 5; 2% Proposition 43). Eighty-six percent are most interested in one of the nine citizens’ initiatives, with about half expressing the most interest in Proposition 39 (23%; Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) and Proposition 40 (22%; Imposes One-Time Tax). There are partisan divides in interest in Proposition 39 (13% Democrat, 47% Republican, 16% independents) and Proposition 40 (27% Democrats, 13% Republicans, 21% independents). Since the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), the share of those most interested in Proposition 40 has increased (16% to 22%).
Citizens’ Initiatives on the November Ballot
In addition to the five legislative measures, voters are weighing in on nine citizens’ initiatives. Overwhelming majorities of California likely voters say that the voter information guide, which is mailed to voters by the California Secretary of State, is very (40%) or somewhat useful (48%; 12% not too useful). Most are very (26%) or somewhat satisfied (59%) with the information that is available to voters about citizens’ initiatives on the state ballot (14% not satisfied).
After reading the ballot title and label for Proposition 3 (Extending Tax on High Incomes), which would make temporary voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 permanent, a majority of likely voters in the state say they would vote yes; four in ten would vote no. Findings were similar in September 2026 (58% yes, 40% no). Today, most Democrats and independents support Proposition 3, while most Republicans oppose. Likely voters who earn less than $40,000 (77%), are age 18 to 34 (73%), or are renters (69%) are among the most likely to say they would vote yes. Majorities across regions are in support, though Central Valley residents are more divided (51% yes, 48% no).
Proposition 37 (Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Home-Buyers), which would authorize $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible California residents fixed-rate mortgages for newly constructed homes below $1.5 million, is supported by about two in three likely voters (65% yes, 32% no). Support was similar in September (61% yes, 35% no). Majorities of Democrats (80%) and independents (54%) are in support; Republicans are more divided (47% yes, 51% no). Majorities across demographic and regional groups say they would vote yes on Proposition 37, and support declines with rising age and income.
A majority of likely voters (57%) would vote yes on Proposition 38 (Authorizes Bonds For Immunology Medical Research), which would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds. About four in ten would vote no (41%). The share in support is similar to a month ago (55% yes, September 2026). Today, partisans are divided (70% Democrats, 53% independents, 37% Republicans) and majorities across regions and demographic groups are in support of Proposition 38.
Fewer than half of likely voters in the state would vote yes (41%, 58% no) on Proposition 39 (Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) which would invalidate mail ballots that do not have the last four digits of a government-issued identification number written on the envelope and prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Shares were similar a month ago (43% yes, 55% no). Today, most Republicans would vote yes (82%), most Democrats would vote no (84%), and independents are divided (48% yes, 50% no). Majorities across most demographic groups would vote no, except for likely voters whose highest level of education is a high school diploma, who are more divided (48% yes, 49% no).
Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax), which would impose a 5 percent tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion, is supported by 46 percent of likely voters, while 52 percent would vote no. A slim majority was in support in September (52% yes, 46% no). Today, over six in ten Democrats would vote yes, compared to four in ten independents and about two in ten Republicans. Likely voters who are younger (70% 18 to 34), earn less than $40,000 (64%), are Latino (58%), or reside in Los Angeles (53%) are among the most likely to support this proposition.
Likely voters are divided on Proposition 41 (Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), which would nullify state taxes enacted after January 1 this year that exempt their revenues from the voter-approved state spending limit and requires audits of programs funded by new special taxes (48% yes, 49% no). Support was similar in September (51% yes, 44% no). Today, most Republicans and independents support Proposition 41, compared to about three in ten Democrats. Support varies across demographic and regional groups.
A slim majority of likely voters would vote yes (51%, 47% no) on Proposition 42 (Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes), which would prohibit new state taxes imposed on the ownership of personal property other than real estate. Support was similar a month ago (54% yes, 43% no). Today, most Republicans and independents would vote yes, while most Democrats would vote no. The share in support varies across demographic and regional groups.
Just a quarter of likely voters would vote yes (25%, 71% no) on Proposition 44 (Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services), which would impose penalties on nonprofit community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations that spend less than 90 percent of revenue on program services. A majority was opposed in September (34% yes, 61% no). Today, six in ten or more across partisan, demographic, and regional groups would vote no.
Likely voters are divided (46% yes, 50% no) on Proposition 45 (Modifies Environmental Review), which would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Views were similar a month ago (49% yes, 46% no). A majority of Republicans would vote yes, while a majority of Democrats (54%) and half of independents (50%) would vote no. The shares in support vary across partisan, demographic, and regional groups.
State of the State
Ahead of the November election, about four in ten adults (45%) and likely voters (38%) choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as the most important issue facing people in California today. Fewer choose housing costs and availability (12% adults, 13% likely voters). Cost of living is most likely to be chosen as the state’s top issue across parties, regions, and demographic groups.
When asked about the economic outlook for the next 12 months, most Californians are pessimistic, with three in four adults (77%) and likely voters (79%) expecting bad economic times. Seven in ten Californians have held this view since 2025. Today, two in three or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups are pessimistic.
Californians are also pessimistic about the outlook for the state, with about six in ten or fewer adults (59%) and likely voters (55%) saying the state is heading in the wrong direction. At least half of Californians have said the state is heading in the wrong direction since June 2023 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2023/). About half or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups—except for Democrats (35%)—hold this pessimistic view.
Nearly all Californians view housing costs as a problem in their part of California, with a solid majority seeing them as a big problem (64%) and three in ten saying they are somewhat of a problem (32%). Just 4 percent say housing affordability is not a problem. Across regions, San Francisco Bay Area residents (71%) are the most likely to say housing costs are a big problem, while Central Valley residents (50%) are the least likely (Inland Empire: 68%, Los Angeles: 67%, Orange County/San Diego: 64%). The view that housing affordability is a big problem is widely held by about six in ten or more across parties and demographic groups.
With inflation on the rise again, most Californians continue to feel they are falling behind. Today, about three in four California adults (76%) and likely voters (73%) say their income is not keeping up with inflation, similar to results in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (71% adults, 67% likely voters). This view is widely held, with seven in ten or more adults across regions and demographic groups saying their income has not kept up. This view is also shared across party lines (74% Democrats, 71% Republicans, 76% independents).
As Governor Newsom approaches the last months of his tenure—and as speculation about his political future swirls—just under half of adults and likely voters approve of his job performance (47% adults, 49% likely voters). Until now, majorities of Californians have approved of the governor since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, about seven in ten Democrats, four in ten independents, and about one in ten Republicans approve of the governor. There are also regional differences: a majority of residents in the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles approve, compared to fewer than half in the other regions.
Half or fewer adults and likely voters approve of the state legislature (42% adults, 46% likely voters) and the state legislators representing their assembly and senate districts (43% adults, 48% likely voters). About half of Californians have approved of the legislature since last October (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/), and views of state legislators were similar in May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/). Today, about six in ten Democrats approve of the state legislature and their own legislators, compared to nearly four in ten independents and fewer than one in five Republicans.
When asked about their confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections, six in ten likely voters have a great deal (42%) or quite a lot (21%) of confidence, while nearly four in ten have some confidence (15%) or very little confidence (22%). Seven in ten likely voters (71%)—with partisans divided—think it’s a good thing that a vote-by-mail ballot is mailed to every active registered voter before each election.
State of the Nation
Asked about the most important problem facing the US today, Californians are most likely to choose the economy, unemployment, and jobs (26%), followed by threats to democratic norms (18%) and corruption (14%). Across partisan groups, Democrats are most likely to choose threats to democratic norms (29%), while the economy is the top choice among independents (32%) and Republicans (25%). The economy is the top national issue across most regions and demographic groups.
A record-high share (82%) of California adults say the US is headed in the wrong direction (79% likely voters). Most Democrats (95%) and independents (85%) hold this view, whereas Republicans are divided (51% wrong direction, 48% right direction). Three in four or more across regions and demographic groups say the country is headed in the wrong direction. Californians (82%) are more likely to hold this pessimistic view than adults nationwide (72%), according to an October ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/ABC-Post-Ipsos%20Trend%20Topline%2010.21.pdf) poll.
Only about three in ten adults say that people who share their political views in the US are extremely (9%) or very (22%) free to express them (likely voters: 11% extremely, 24% very). Conversely, similar shares believe that people who share their political views are a little (16% adults, 14% likely voters) or not at all free (13% adults, 11% likely voters) to openly express them. Three in ten adults and a third of likely voters (36%) believe people who share their views are somewhat free to express them. Views were similar among adults nationwide in a June Pew Research Center (https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/2026/09/15/americans-value-press-freedom-but-differ-on-its-limits/) survey.
Most California adults say freedom of the press is at least somewhat important to the well-being of society (92% adults, 95% likely voters). While majorities across partisan groups share this view, Democrats (68%) are far more likely than independents (49%) and Republicans (27%) to say freedom of the press is extremely important.
When asked about the way democracy is working in the US, just three in ten adults (5% very, 26% somewhat) and likely voters (7% very, 25% somewhat) say they are satisfied. About seven in ten say they are not satisfied with democracy in the US (adults: 39% not too, 29% not at all; likely voters: 37% not too, 31% not at all). About three in four Democrats (79%) and independents (74%) express dissatisfaction, while a majority of Republicans (59%) are satisfied. Six in ten or more across regions and demographic groups are dissatisfied.
About two in ten California adults (21%) approve of the way Donald Trump is handling his job as president (26% likely voters)—a record low across both terms of his presidency. For comparison, Donald Trump’s approval rating stood at 29 percent in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-1018.pdf). Today, overwhelming majorities of Democrats and independents disapprove of the president, while seven in ten Republicans approve.
Fewer approve of the way the US Congress is handling its job (16% adults, 17% likely voters). Two in ten or fewer have approved of Congress since June 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2025/). Today, majorities across partisan groups disapprove of the US Congress.
Three in ten adults (30%) and about four in ten likely voters (38%) approve of the way their own representative to the US House of Representatives is handling the job. Shares are similar among Californians who currently live in a Democratic-held seat and a Republican-held seat. Four in ten or fewer across regions and demographic groups approve of the way their own House representative is handling the job.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (72%) disapprove of US military action against Iran. Most Democrats (94%) and independents (74%) disapprove, while about two in three Republicans approve (65%). About two in three or more across regions and demographic groups disapprove. California adults are more likely than adults nationwide (61%) to disapprove, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/Reuters%20Ipsos%20News%20Issue%20Survey%20October%202026%20Topline_3.pdf) poll.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (71%) disapprove of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing. Overall, seven in ten or more adults have disapproved since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, most Democrats (95%) and independents (75%) disapprove, while most Republicans (72%) approve of ICE. Solid majorities across demographic and regional groups disapprove.
About two in three likely voters say they are very (25%) or somewhat (40%) confident that votes for Congress will be accurately counted nationwide. The share who are very confident has dropped from October 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2024/) (38%).

Methodology
The PPIC Statewide Survey has been conducted since April 1998 to provide a voice for the public, inform policymakers, encourage discussion, and raise awareness of critical issues facing California. The coauthors of this report include survey director Mark Baldassare, who holds the Miller Chair in Public Policy; associate survey director and research fellow Dean Bonner; survey analyst Lauren Mora, who was the project manager for this survey; and survey analyst Deja Thomas. The Californians and Their Government survey on state, local, and national issues is supported with funding from the Arjay R. and Frances F. Miller Foundation. The PPIC Statewide Survey invites input, comments, and suggestions from policy and public opinion experts and from its own advisory committee members, but survey methods, questions, and content are determined solely by PPIC’s survey team. We thank Paul Lewis and Eric McGhee for helpful reviews of an earlier report draft.
Findings in this report are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. The survey was conducted from October 16–22, 2026.
The survey was conducted by Ipsos, using its online KnowledgePanel, in English and Spanish according to respondents’ preferences. KnowledgePanel members are recruited through probability-based sampling and include both those with internet access and those without. KnowledgePanel provides internet access for those who do not have it and, if needed, a device to access the internet when they join the panel. KnowledgePanel members are primarily recruited using address-based sampling (ABS) methodology, which improves population coverage, particularly for hard-to-reach populations such as young adults and minority groups. ABS-recruited Latinos are supplemented with a dual-frame random digit dialing (RDD) sampling methodology that targets telephone exchanges associated with areas with a higher concentration of Latinos to provide the capability to conduct representative online surveys with Latinos, including those who speak only Spanish. KnowledgePanel’s recruitment was originally based on a national RDD frame and switched to the primarily ABS-based methodology in 2009. KnowledgePanel includes households with landlines and cell phones, including those with cell phones only and those without phones. ABS allows probability-based sampling of addresses from the US Postal Service’s Delivery Sequence File (DSF). Proposition 37
Create low-cost mortgages for homebuyers
California’s Housing Finance Agency would be able (but not required) to borrow up to $25 billion to help would-be homebuyers purchase newly constructed houses and condos. These loans could provide up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, leaving buyers with a cash down payment of 3% if paired with a typical mortgage — $24,000 for an $800,000 home. Homebuyers would repay the loan in monthly installments to private lenders. Anyone earning up to twice the area’s median income would be eligible. Private lenders, not taxpayers, would be on the hook if homebuyers default. It was placed on the ballot by a coalition of real estate interests and labor unions.

Summary
Support
House hunters can expect to face a down payment equal to 20% of the value of a home. In California, where $700,000 for a fixer-upper is considered a steal in much of the state, that’s not feasible for most people. This loan program will put the dream of homeownership within reach of the middle class without costing taxpayers a dime.
Oppose
Some opponents argue that state government should not be involved in the mortgage lending market and note that the measure won’t do much to address the underlying reasons that housing in California is so expensive. Others note that while it would help more people buy homes, it would only do so by allowing them to go into even deeper debt.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

Tax the Top, Fix Housing, Back Becerra: Cost of Living Drives California’s Vote, AIMSA Poll Finds
Tax the Top, Fix Housing, Back Becerra: Cost of Living Drives California’s Vote, AIMSA Poll Finds
Business Wire
27-10-2026

Seven in ten voters name an economic issue as the state’s top problem. Majorities back extending taxes on high incomes and borrowing for housing, the billionaire tax is a toss-up, and Becerra leads by 24 points even though fewer than half of voters say California is on the right track.
SAN DIEGO: California’s election is being decided at the kitchen table. Seven in ten likely voters name an economic issue as the state’s top problem - cost of living (38%), housing (19%), and the economy and jobs (12%) - and their ballot choices suggest they want the bill sent to the top, according to a new poll by AIMSA, distributed by Quadratín California.
The survey of 2,000 likely voters, conducted October 19–24, finds a consistent pattern on the ballot. Proposition 3, which extends taxes on high incomes, has 56% support; Proposition 37, loans for middle-income homebuyers, 59%; and Proposition 1, affordable housing bonds, 54%. At the same time, 50% back Proposition 42, which would ban state taxes on personal property. The pattern suggests voters favor measures whose cost falls on a narrow group of taxpayers or that expand access to housing, and resist taxes that could reach their own households.
“The message from California voters is clear: affordability and economic opportunity come first,” said Tayde Aburto, President of the Hispanic Chamber of E-Commerce (HISCEC). “Behind these numbers are families working to make ends meet and small business owners navigating rising costs.”
The most closely watched measure, Proposition 40, a one-time tax on billionaires, leads 50% to 44%, a margin the report places within the poll’s range of error. Its outcome is likely to resonate well beyond California.
Politically, the poll reveals a paradox: only 45% of voters say the state is headed in the right direction, yet Democrat Xavier Becerra leads Republican Steve Hilton 58% to 34%. President Donald Trump’s approval among the state’s likely voters is just 29%, compared with 50% for Governor Gavin Newsom, suggesting the race is being shaped as much by views of Washington as of Sacramento. The race appears largely settled: 24% have already voted and only 13% say they could change their minds.
For voters of Mexican origin, the affordability squeeze crosses the border. Seventy-one percent of Latino voters were born in the U.S., yet 29% send remittances to their country of origin and 34% chose to answer in Spanish: for nearly three in ten, one household budget supports two economies. Mexican-origin voters back Becerra 66% to 25%, while Latinos of other origins vote almost exactly like the state as a whole (58% to 32%). And while 52% of Latino voters approve of Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, only 41% approve of the U.S.–Mexico relationship.
Leo Espinoza, President of Quadratín California, said the findings place the voices of Latino and Mexican-origin voters - a community with strong ties to Mexico - at the center of the conversation about the state’s future.
A second wave of the AIMSA survey, in the field since October 26, will show whether the billionaire tax and other close measures move in the final stretch. The full report, with results by region, age, sex and party, all 14 propositions, and the module on Latino and Mexican-origin voters, is available to journalists. Jesús Javier García Ruiz, Director of AIMSA, is available for interviews.
Methodology
AIMSA independently directed, conducted and financed the study; Quadratín California is the media partner and HISCEC supports outreach. The survey combines 1,200 SMS-to-web interviews linked to the voter file and 800 online panel interviews, in English and Spanish, across seven regions, with an oversample of 800 Latino voters. The 95% credibility interval is ±3 points statewide and ±4.5 among Latinos, larger for subgroups such as voters of Mexican origin. Results are not a forecast.

Will Prop. 37 Make Homeownership More Affordable? It’s Not Guaranteed
Understanding How Proposition 37 Could Affect Homeownership Affordability
August 2026 | By Monica Davalos (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/monica-davalos/), Nishi Nair (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/nishi-nair/), and Kristin Schumacher (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/kristin-schumacher/)
Print Report
key takeaway
Proposition 37 on the November 2026 ballot would establish a “middle-class” homebuyer downpayment assistance program, funded with up to $25 billion in revenue bonds. This assistance could only be used to purchase newly built homes or newly created housing units converted from nonresidential buildings, where the buyer is the first purchaser. The program is intended to be self-sustaining because participating homebuyers — not the state — would ultimately repay the bonds through their mortgage payments.

Who Supports and Opposes Prop. 37?
Supporting homeownership is an important strategy for promoting economic security and wealth building. However, it is unclear whether Prop. 37 would meaningfully help “middle class” Californians who face the greatest barriers to homeownership to afford a home.
As Prop. 37 would be financed through revenue bonds — which do not require voter approval — the program proposed by this initiative could have been enacted legislatively or a comparable program could have been established by the California Finance Housing Agency. Prop. 37 is a citizens’ initiative spearheaded by former California Senate Majority Leader and Assembly Speaker Bob Hertzberg.
What Would Prop. 37 Do?
The Middle Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026 (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0013A1%20%28%26quot%3BCalifornia%20Middle-Class%20Homeownership%20and%20Family%20Home%20Construction%20Act%20of%202026%26quot%3B%29_0.pdf) would direct the California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) to establish a middle-class homebuyer downpayment assistance program, funded with up to $25 billion in revenue bonds. The new program would:
Provide up to 17% of the purchase price toward the down payment , which could only be used to purchase new homes or newly created housing units converted from nonresidential buildings, where the buyer is the first purchaser.
Require the buyer to put down at least 3% of the purchase price toward the down payment. Combined with the 17% state downpayment assistance, this would reach 20% of the home’s purchase price and eliminates the need for private mortgage insurance. A conventional first mortgage would cover the remaining amount.
Require the downpayment assistance to be provided as a loan, not a grant, which recipients are likely to pay back monthly as a fixed-rate second mortgage . This would be in addition to the homebuyer’s monthly payments on their conventional first mortgage.
Allow applicants to have incomes up to 200% of the Area Median Income (AMI) , which varies by region.
Cap the maximum home purchase price at roughly $1 million to $1.5 million, depending on the county and other factors. This is equivalent to a $170,000-$255,000 downpayment assistance cap per home.
Not require applicants to be first-time or first-generation home buyers , nor would recipients owe the state any equity gained in their home. These are requirements of comparable state downpayment assistance programs the state currently operates.
Allow home builders to become “qualified builders,” and have their developments automatically qualify for the program if they meet specified labor and enforcement standards.
How Would Income Eligibility for Prop. 37’s Downpayment Assistance Vary Across California Counties?
Prop. 37 would make a broad group of Californians eligible for downpayment assistance by allowing family incomes not exceeding 200% of Area Median Income (AMI) to qualify, a threshold that extends well beyond established downpayment assistance programs.
AMI represents the midpoint of family incomes in a specific area, adjusted for household size. In other words, half of households in an area have incomes that exceed 100% AMI and half have incomes below that level, so 200% AMI is roughly double what a typical family makes in the area. The limit is tied to local incomes, so whether a family income would qualify for Prop. 37’s downpayment assistance would vary significantly across California.
For example, a Budget Center analysis of Census Bureau data shows that a family of four earning up to $166,800 annually in Madera County or up to $375,800 annually in Santa Clara County could each qualify for assistance. However, the final dollar amounts would be set by CalHFA if Prop. 37 is approved by voters.
How Is Prop. 37 Different from California’s Existing Downpayment Assistance Programs?
California operates several (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/homebuyer/programs/index.htm) statewide homeownership programs through CalHFA, but Prop. 37 would take a different approach that could hit family budgets harder, as participants are likely to pay back the downpayment assistance monthly as a fixed-rate second mortgage.
For example, CalHFA’s MyHome Assistance Program (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/homebuyer/programs/myhome.htm) and the Dream for All Shared Appreciation Loan (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/dream/) program both provide downpayment assistance through deferred “silent second (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/myaccount/faqs.htm)” loans (also known as silent second mortgages). MyHome charges 1% simple interest on the assistance; Dream for All accrues no interest, but requires a 15% or 20% share of the home’s appreciation to go to the state. Under both programs, nothing is due on these silent second mortgages until the homeowner sells, refinances, or pays off the first mortgage. This ensures that the downpayment assistance doesn’t compete with the first mortgage, groceries, utility bills, or other basic needs in a family’s monthly budget.
Prop. 37’s approach is likely to require monthly payments. This is because CalHFA would issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds, and by law those bonds must be repaid from the proceeds of the program itself — meaning the principal and interest of the second mortgages CalHFA issues. The second mortgages would need to generate steady, ongoing revenue to pay the debt from the revenue bonds. Language in the measure also states “a borrower may request a temporary hardship deferral of monthly interest payments on its middle-class homeownership loan,” further alluding to its intended structure.

Under Prop. 37, the second mortgage payment could also likely carry higher interest rates above conventional first mortgage rates. Although the measure states the intent to provide below-market downpayment assistance financing, it doesn’t guarantee it. The interest rate on the second mortgages would ultimately depend on the terms under which the bonds are issued and market conditions at the time of implementation, which are largely outside CalHFA’s control.
Revenue bonds that finance second mortgages are inherently riskier for investors because if a homeowner defaults, the first mortgage gets repaid before the second, leaving the bond investors more exposed to loss. Investors may therefore require a higher return to compensate for that additional risk, which could increase the interest rate on the second mortgage. This means Prop. 37’s second mortgage rate could land above the roughly 6.5% conventional first-mortgage rates buyers already face today. CalHFA wouldn’t set the actual rate or terms on the second mortgage until implementation, so the interest rate cannot be known before voters decide on Prop. 37.
Ultimately, while Prop. 37 could help get homebuyers to a 20% downpayment to avoid private mortgage insurance, the monthly repayment costs for the second mortgage could erode much of the benefit the downpayment assistance was meant to provide.
Would Prop. 37 Reach “Middle-Class” Californians Facing the Greatest Barriers to Homeownership?
Prop. 37 would make a broad range of households eligible for downpayment assistance, but income eligibility alone does not determine who can realistically purchase a home. Racial and ethnic disparities in income (https://www.ppic.org/publication/income-inequality-in-california/#:~:text=Overall%2C%20the%20highest,without%20college%20degrees.), wealth (https://apps.urban.org/features/wealth-inequality-charts/#:~:text=Wealth%20gaps%20by%20race%20and%20ethnicity%20are%20large.), credit access (https://www.epi.org/publication/chasing-the-dream-of-equity/#:~:text=Despite%20the%20bill%E2%80%99s%20intention%20to%20expand%20credit%20access%2C%20Black%20applicants%20are%20consistently%20more%20likely%20to%20be%20denied%20loans%20than%20applicants%20from%20other%20racial%20groups%20(), and housing affordability (https://www.car.org/aboutus/mediacenter/newsreleases/2026releases/HAI2025byEthnicity#:~:text=Meanwhile%2C%20only%2011%20percent%20of%20Black%20households%20and%2011%20percent%20of%20Hispanic/Latino%20households%20had%20the%20same%20ability.) mean that not all eligible families across California may be positioned to benefit from the program as proposed.
Prop. 37 would require the buyer to put down at least 3% of the purchase price, which would still be unattainable for many Californians. For example:
A house that costs $500,000 would require a 3% down payment of $15,000.
A house that costs $700,000 would require a 3% down payment of $21,000.
These upfront costs could be out of reach for many families, with the result that Prop. 37’s assistance could largely benefit families with incomes toward the higher end of the eligibility range. According to the Public Policy Institute of California, the median amount in Californians’ checking and savings accounts was just over $18,000 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/0525ttr-appendix.pdf) in 2025 dollars. This means that a 3% down payment could still almost or entirely clear out most or all of what an average family has in checkings and savings.
Prop. 37 could also reinforce economic, racial, and ethnic inequities in homeownership. The measure is intended to help “middle class” Californians, roughly defined as those with incomes between 80% to 200% AMI. White families are overrepresented among middle- and upper-middle-income Californians (46%), compared to their share of all California families (42%).
In contrast, Black and Latinx families are underrepresented in this “middle class” income range. This means that white families could disproportionately benefit from this program — even though white households already make up the largest share of homeowners (https://www.ppic.org/blog/californias-renters/#:~:text=Within%20the%20state,a%20college%20degree.) in the state, while Black and Latinx renter households face disproportionately high housing costs (https://calhousingpartnership.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/CHP_State-Housing-Needs-Report-2025.pdf).
Prop. 37 does not require applicants to be first-time or first-generation home buyers, further exacerbating equity concerns. Black and brown communities have been historically excluded from building wealth (https://apps.urban.org/features/wealth-inequality-charts/) and accumulating assets, making the barrier to entering the housing market even more pronounced. Families of color face occupational segregation (https://www.americanprogress.org/article/occupational-segregation-in-america/) that pushes them into lower-paying jobs. They are also less likely to inherit generational wealth (https://budgetmodel.wharton.upenn.edu/p/2021-12-17-inheritances-by-race/), and are more likely to be renters. (https://www.ppic.org/blog/californias-renters/#:~:text=Within%20the%20state,a%20college%20degree.) These factors make it substantially more difficult to save for a down payment, even at similar income levels. Additionally, data limitations often mask significant disparities in homeownership (https://www.urban.org/urban-wire/why-does-homeownership-vary-so-widely-within-aapi-community) access across racial and ethnic groups, especially among Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander Californians.
Could Prop. 37 Encourage Sprawl and Harm the Environment?
By restricting downpayment assistance to newly built homes or newly created housing units converted from nonresidential buildings, Prop. 37 could push more “middle-class” housing onto land that’s not well suited for housing. Much of the land in California best suited for housing has already been developed (https://shou.senate.ca.gov/system/files/2025-02/recent-leg-actions-factsheet-updated-feb-2025_0.pdf), leaving remaining areas that are often far from job centers, prone to wildfire,environmentally sensitive, or important for agriculture.
While existing state down payment assistance programs are not immune to these concerns because they can also be used to purchase new homes, Prop. 37 goes further by limiting assistance exclusively to newly constructed homes. As a result, Prop. 37 could further direct “middle-class” housing demand toward suburban and exurban areas. This is a critical deviation from infill development — building on denser, already developed land — which has been the focus of state affordable housing and environmental efforts.
This pattern of building housing on the periphery of cities (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2936977/#:~:text=IN%20THE%20LAST,a%20city%2C%20is) is known as urban sprawl (https://www.urban.org/sites/default/files/2024-05/Patterns_of_Sprawl_in_Fresno_and_the_Central_San_Joaquin_Valley.pdf) and carries various environmental and equity considerations. Development in more suburban and inland areas can push Californians further from job centers, increasing their commute times and making it difficult to travel without a car (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2936977/#:~:text=People%20who%20live%20in%20large%20metropolitan%20areas%20often%20find%20it%20difficult%20to%20travel%20even%20short%20distances%20without%20using%20an%20automobile%2C%20because%20of%20the%20remoteness%20of%20residential%20areas%20and%20inadequate%20availability%20of%20mass%20transit%2C%20walkways%2C%20or%20bike%20paths). It may also encourage development in areas on the outskirts of cities that may cause new homes to infringe upon natural habitats and important agricultural lands (https://www.urban.org/sites/default/files/2024-05/Patterns_of_Sprawl_in_Fresno_and_the_Central_San_Joaquin_Valley.pdf), especially in areas like the Central Valley. Sprawl can also lead to divestment from urban areas (http://urban.org/sites/default/files/2024-05/Patterns_of_Sprawl_in_Fresno_and_the_Central_San_Joaquin_Valley.pdf), which are often composed of communities of color, and concentrate investment in higher-income, suburban neighborhoods, further exacerbating racial and income inequality across the state.
What Other Homeownership Costs Could Come with Prop. 37’s New-Construction Requirement?
Prop. 37’s new construction requirement could steer homebuyers toward housing with higher out-of-pocket costs on top of their monthly mortgage payments. Unlike existing state down payment assistance programs, which can be used to purchase both new and existing homes, Prop. 37 would limit assistance to newly constructed homes. New construction homes are more likely to come with homeowners association (HOA) dues, Mello-Roos assessments, and home insurance challenges.
HOA fees are far more common in new homes as nearly 70% of newly built homes (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-housing-hoa-fees/) listed for sale nationally in 2024 were subject to HOA dues, compared with about 38% of existing homes. In California, more than a third of residents live in an HOA — including about 65% of all California homeowners. The average monthly fee is $280 (https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2025/09/condo-hoa-fees.html), and fees can rise up to 20% annually without a homeowner vote under current state law.
New construction in undeveloped areas of California also often comes with Mello-Roos (https://www.treasurer.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2025-10/2023_1.pdf) special tax assessments, which fund infrastructure like roads, schools, and utilities in newly developed areas and are layered on top of regular property taxes — typically adding another monthly fee to new-build homes for years.
